prompt: A service has normal traffic of ~20 req/s at night and ~400 req/s at midday. A static-threshold alert fires below 50 req/s. What does this threshold actually do?
choices: Fires correctly at both night and day because 50 is between the two extremes
False-positives every night (normal nighttime traffic is below 50) and false-negatives on a real midday drop like 400 to 220 (still above 50)
Never fires at all, because req/s never crosses exactly 50
Only fires during real incidents, since 50 is well below the daytime baseline

prompt: In the seasonal baseline detector built in this module, why use the median and MAD (median absolute deviation) of past same-slot samples instead of the mean and standard deviation?
choices: Median and MAD are always numerically smaller, which makes thresholds easier to pick
Mean and standard deviation can't be computed on time-series data
Median and MAD are far less distorted by a single outlier week in the history window, so one past bad incident doesn't quietly raise the baseline and desensitize the detector
Median and MAD require fewer historical samples to compute than mean and standard deviation

prompt: What does the PromQL `offset 7d` modifier do in the expression `sum(rate(http_requests_total[5m] offset 7d))`?
choices: Delays the alert from firing for 7 days after the condition becomes true
Evaluates the same rate expression as if the current time were shifted back 7 days, letting you compare now against the same point last week
Averages the metric over a rolling 7-day window
Drops any data points older than 7 days from the query

prompt: In the worked LLM root-cause-analysis example (checkout latency spike traced to a dropped database index), what was the actual prerequisite that made the LLM's correct answer possible?
choices: The specific LLM model used had been fine-tuned on that company's incident history
Structured, correlated telemetry — a trace pinpointing the slow span, a deploy log naming the exact schema change, and a log line naming the exact slow query
The incident was simple enough that any automated tool would have solved it the same way
The LLM was given direct database access to run EXPLAIN ANALYZE itself

prompt: In the flash-sale / Redis eviction-policy scenario, what was the actual root cause of the latency and error increase?
choices: The checkout-service feature-flag deploy for the new upsell banner
The system simply could not handle 3x normal traffic volume
An eviction-policy change (noeviction to allkeys-lru) with maxmemory left too low, which only caused cache misses once write volume crossed a threshold that the traffic spike reached
An unrelated dependency bump in billing-service

prompt: Why is temporal correlation between a deploy (or traffic change) and an incident's onset time not sufficient evidence of causation, as shown in the flash-sale example?
choices: Timestamps in distributed systems are never reliable enough to compare at all

Two different changes can both correlate with the same onset time while only one combination of a long-dormant latent condition plus a new trigger is the real cause -- distinguishing that requires a counterfactual test, not just matching timestamps
Correlation is only invalid when more than three changes happen on the same day
LLMs are structurally incapable of mentioning timestamps in their reasoning

prompt: According to this module, what is the strongest concrete reason human judgment must remain the gate on automated/LLM-assisted incident diagnosis, even when the proposed root cause sounds confident and well-evidenced?
choices: LLMs cannot format their output clearly enough for on-call engineers to read under pressure

Confident, fluent phrasing is not evidence of correctness, and acting automatically on a plausible-but-wrong hypothesis can trigger costly or irreversible actions that a human, weighing business context and blast radius, would not take on an unverified guess
Automated systems are legally barred from touching production infrastructure in most organizations
LLMs cannot process structured logs or trace data at all
